title: Scientists Decipher Genome of Coffee Plant
main_content:
The genetic sequence of the coffee plant, Robusta, has been deciphered by an international team of scientists. Robusta accounts for about one-third of the coffee consumed worldwide.

By laying bare the plant’s genetic building blocks, researchers will be able to improve breeding as well as genetically modify it.

Most surprising to geneticists was discovering the genes for caffeine.

Scientists have speculated the plant evolved a mechanism for producing caffeine to lure insect pollinators, just as people can get addicted to coffee. It’s also been thought that caffeine, which can be toxic, is a defense against leaf-destroying insects.

The researchers determined that coffee’s caffeine genes are not related to the genes responsible for caffeine in the cacao tree, the source of chocolate. That they developed separately indicates that caffeine is a valuable evolutionary asset.

Having mapped the coffee plant’s genome, researchers say they could potentially make plants resistant to climate change and eliminate caffeine in coffee, producing a better tasting brew for those who only drink the decaffeinated variety.

It’s estimated that 2.25 billion cups of coffee are consumed each day, making it the principal agricultural crop in many tropical countries.

The genetic blueprint of the coffee plant Robusta is published in the journal Science.

questions.question: How popular is Robusta worldwide?
options: It accounts for nearly half of all coffee consumed globally.
It is the least cultivated coffee species in major coffee-producing countries.
It represents about one-third of the coffee consumed worldwide.
It is primarily consumed in Europe and North America.
questions.answer: It represents about one-third of the coffee consumed worldwide.

questions.question: What did scientists discover about caffeine?
options: Caffeine genes in coffee are identical to those in the cacao tree.
The plant evolved to produce caffeine solely for human consumption.
Genes for caffeine in Robusta developed separately from those in cacao.
Caffeine in coffee serves no evolutionary purpose.
questions.answer: Genes for caffeine in Robusta developed separately from those in cacao.

questions.question: What are the consequences of mapping the coffee plant’s genome?
options: It allows for the elimination of all caffeine in coffee production.
Researchers can make the coffee plant resistant to climate change and target caffeine levels.
It increases the production of Robusta coffee in tropical countries.
Scientists have found a way to enhance the toxicity of caffeine against pests.
questions.answer: Researchers can make the coffee plant resistant to climate change and target caffeine levels.
